title: Accurate noise spectroscopy using quantum sensing ensembles
authors: Dhilan T Vallury, Nikolai Dontschuk, Alexander M Jakob, Alexander J Healey, David A Simpson
abstract: Noise spectroscopy with quantum sensors is a powerful tool for characterising the properties of the sensor environment and detecting critical magnetic phenomena. While replacing single sensors with large ensembles promises substantial gains in measurement sensitivity and field of view, the output becomes difficult to interpret when there is a variable coupling to targets across the sensing ensemble. In this work we present an analysis procedure for accessing the true source noise spectrum using ensemble coherence from dynamical decoupling measurements. We show that sequence timing plays a dual role in ensemble noise spectroscopy, setting both the frequency selectivity and the weighted collection of signal across the ensemble, and demonstrate how incorporation of the coupling distribution allows accurate parameter extraction of the noise. We apply this procedure to a model system, shallow nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond, and show that consistent information about the spectral character of MHz-range surface noise can be obtained from two sensing ensembles featuring distinct depth distributions. Our results pave the way for using large quantum sensor ensembles for quantitative, broadband noise spectroscopy, with straightforward extension to other solid-state and molecular sensing platforms.
summary: This paper details a rigorous analysis procedure for extracting the true source noise spectrum from measurements taken using large ensembles of quantum sensors. By mathematically incorporating the spatial distribution of the sensors, the authors overcome ambiguities inherent in ensemble averaging. This methodology paves the way for quantitative, broadband noise characterization using solid-state quantum platforms.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately reconstructing the true source noise spectrum $S_0(\omega)$ from ensemble coherence measurements $\langle C(T) angle$ when the sensing ensemble has a variable coupling depth distribution.
main_result: The authors present an analysis procedure that incorporates the coupling distribution $P(d)$ to accurately extract the source noise spectrum, demonstrating its applicability to NV centers in diamond.
method: The method involves analyzing the ensemble coherence decay, which is modeled as an integral over the depth distribution, and using approximations (like the short-T limit) to invert the measured decay into the underlying noise spectrum.
model_or_system: The system studied is quantum sensing ensembles, specifically using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. The noise environment is modeled as separable, $S(\omega, d) = S_0(\omega)D(d)$, where $D(d)$ describes depth variation.
key_observables: Ensemble coherence $\langle C(T) angle$, the source noise spectrum $S_0(\omega)$, and the depth distribution $P(d)$.
important_parameters: Measurement time $T$, depth distribution parameters (e.g., depth range, width), and noise frequency $\omega$.
main_assumptions: Key assumptions include modeling the noise as separable across depth and assuming specific functional forms for the depth distribution (e.g., $d^{-3}$ scaling). A major limitation is the inherent ambiguity between the amplitude of $S_0$ and the scale of $P(d)$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the accuracy of fitting methods for depth profiles and source spectra, comparing 'naive' fitting against reconstruction methods that account for the depth distribution. Specific comparisons are made between 2 keV and 4 keV ensembles.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework for ensemble averaging, analyzes the ambiguities in parameter extraction, and then applies this procedure to model systems (like NV centers) to demonstrate the quantitative extraction of broadband noise spectra.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to AMO physics as it deals with using quantum systems (NV centers) as highly sensitive probes to characterize the local electromagnetic environment (noise spectroscopy), a core topic in quantum sensing and open quantum systems.
